title: The Dragonfly's Eye: My Virtual Camera (AI)
description:
A late book by the German filmmaker and writer Alexander Kluge that takes AI image generation as a new kind of camera and asks what its pictures can and cannot show.

Kluge looks at the quirks of these images, where chance and error produce what the publisher calls subjunctive forms: open images that are hard to place. The 480-page pocket-format hardcover builds its stories around them, moving between cases as unlike as East German phantom pregnancies and present-day political figures. The AI works as a virtual camera that tells and re-imagines space through pictures. Spector Books issued it in 2024, with a separate German edition titled Der Konjunktiv der Bilder.

Kluge was born in Halberstadt in 1932 and died in 2026. He signed the 1962 Oberhausen Manifesto and became a leading figure of New German Cinema, with Yesterday Girl (1966) winning a Silver Lion at Venice. From 1987 he produced television through his company dctp, and he wrote theory with Oskar Negt, including Public Sphere and Experience and History and Obstinacy. He received the Georg Büchner Prize in 2003.

title: Goodbye, World! Looking at Art in the Digital Age
description:
A curator's argument that art made and seen in a networked world has to be looked at differently.

Sternberg Press published the 212-page paperback in 2018. Kholeif asks how life and art have changed in the twenty-first century. He treats the internet as a replacement for older ways of picturing the world. John Berger's Ways of Seeing and Alvin Toffler's Future Shock are his stated inspirations. The text mixes memoir with critical analysis of image perception, technology and post-digital practice. It has 195 colour illustrations and was designed by Zak Group.

Kholeif is an Egyptian-born curator and writer. He has worked at the Whitechapel Gallery, HOME Manchester and the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago, and later directed collections at the Sharjah Art Foundation. The book follows You Are Here: Art After the Internet (2014). Art in the Age of Anxiety (2021) and Internet_Art (2023) came after it.

title: antiDATA: la désobéissance numérique. Art et hacktivisme technocritique
description:
A French-language study of artists, hackers and activists who answer the power of digital platforms with acts of disobedience.

Les presses du réel published the 232-page paperback in November 2020 in its Perceptions collection, with 51 colour illustrations. Fourmentraux examines resistance to the dominance of technological innovation through counter-surveillance, tactical media, speculative design and data visualization. Trevor Paglen, Paolo Cirio and Julien Prévieux are among the artists discussed. The book argues that these practices challenge the sovereignty of platforms while writing the histories of code and cryptography into cultural critique.

Fourmentraux holds a doctorate in socio-anthropology and is a professor at Aix-Marseille University. He is an art critic affiliated with AICA and a member of the Centre Norbert Elias. His earlier books on digital culture include Art et Internet (2005) and L'Ère post-média (2012).

title: Digital Art
edition_printrun: Third edition (revised and expanded); World of Art series
description:
A standard survey of digital art from the 1980s onward, in the compact World of Art series, by a curator of new media.

The third edition, revised and expanded, appeared from Thames & Hudson in 2015 as a 272-page paperback with 338 illustrations. It adds recent developments in location-based media, interactive installations, augmented and mixed reality, and tablet technologies. Themes run through the chapters: viewer interaction, artificial intelligence, activism, networks and telepresence. The book also looks at how digital techniques have affected older art forms, and treats internet art, software art, digital installation and virtual reality as established practices.

Christiane Paul is Adjunct Curator of New Media Arts at the Whitney Museum of American Art and is known internationally for curating and teaching new media art. The book is a general history of the field, written for students and readers new to it. Earlier editions exist: the second edition carries ISBN 9780500203989.

title: Entangled Realities: Living with Artificial Intelligence / Leben mit künstlicher Intelligenz
contributors: Felix Stalder (Essay); Matteo Pasquinelli (Essay); Nora N. Khan (Essay)
description:
The catalogue of a 2019 HeK Basel exhibition on how artificial intelligence shapes the world it claims to describe.

The 224-page volume pairs works by artists including James Bridle, Mario Klingemann, Trevor Paglen and Lauren McCarthy with theoretical texts. Felix Stalder writes on the opacity of machine-learning systems. Matteo Pasquinelli traces the history of the algorithm from ancient Indian rituals to the present. Nora N. Khan contributes a dialogue on machine violence. The editors' own essays document the curatorial process and set out the scientific and artistic context of the show.

Sabine Himmelsbach and Boris Magrini edited the book for HeK. The exhibition treated AI as an immature technology that already fires the public imagination, as virtual reality did in the 1990s. Pasquinelli's contribution links the book to his later The Eye of the Master.

title: The Eye of the Master: A Social History of Artificial Intelligence
description:
A history of artificial intelligence that locates its origin in the organisation of labour rather than in the imitation of the human brain.

Pasquinelli argues that the logic of AI comes from the automation of work and from the social relations of the factory, including the surveillance of collective behaviour. The 272-page book follows that line from Babbage's calculating engines and the mechanisation of mental labour through Marx's general intellect, Hayek's epistemology of connectionism and the invention of the perceptron, to current image-recognition systems. It rejects the idea that algorithms could become autonomous.

Matteo Pasquinelli is an associate professor of philosophy of science at Ca' Foscari University in Venice. The Eye of the Master was published by Verso in October 2023 and won the 2024 Deutscher Memorial Prize. His essay on the history of the algorithm also appears in the HeK Basel catalogue Entangled Realities.

title: You Are Here: Art After the Internet
description:
An anthology on how the internet changed the making of art, published as the first major book on what was then called post-internet practice.

The book grew out of the SPACE Art + Technology Programme, a yearlong residency at The White Building in London. It gathers essays and artist projects by about twenty-two contributors, among them James Bridle, Jon Rafman, Zach Blas, Erika Balsom, Sophia Al-Maria and Jennifer Chan, with a foreword by Ed Halter. Artist contributions include work by James Richards, Jamie Shovlin, Jeremy Bailey and Jon Rafman. Writers and artists give first-person accounts of working with and through the internet from the early 2000s onward.

Omar Kholeif curated the 2013 programme at The White Building and edited the volume. It was co-published by Cornerhouse and SPACE in spring 2014, with a cover designed by Sam Ashby. SPACE reports three reprints since publication.
